h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in South Carolina
intro: From the Upstate's mill villages to Columbia's bungalows and the Lowcountry's single houses and piazzas, South Carolina packs very different renovation problems into a small state. Termites are a constant everywhere, heat and humidity drive HVAC and mold decisions, and the coast adds flood zones, salt air and hurricane wind to the list. Genstone Construction renovates houses across South Carolina for real estate investors, mortgage servicers, banks, REITs and investment funds, with active work in Columbia, Charleston and Greenville and the towns around them. We're headquartered in Romeoville, Illinois. In South Carolina, the work is done by vetted, licensed local contractors, and each project has a designated Genstone field manager who coordinates permits, design review, inspections, CL-100 termite reports and lien waivers. Acquisitions can start with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review that estimates repairs and checks the after-repair value before you commit. After that, you get an itemized scope with draws tied to completed work, no upfront payment and a one-year workmanship warranty once you approve the finished project.

sections.h2: South Carolina housing across the Upstate, Midlands and Lowcountry
sections.body:
The Upstate's signature investor stock is its textile mill housing. Greenville's Judson, Poe, Monaghan, Dunean and Brandon villages, along with similar neighborhoods in Spartanburg and smaller towns, hold rows of company-built frame houses on brick piers, with heart pine floors, board walls and central chimneys. Greenville's North Main and Augusta Road add bungalows and revival houses, and post-war brick ranches fill Berea, Taylors and Mauldin.

In the Midlands, Columbia's Elmwood Park, Cottontown, Shandon, Melrose Heights and Wales Garden carry early twentieth-century bungalows and cottages on raised crawlspaces, Olympia and Granby preserve mill houses near the Congaree River, and Dentsville, St. Andrews and Eau Claire supply post-war ranches that anchor rental portfolios.

The Lowcountry is different again. Charleston's peninsula holds single houses, freedman's cottages and double houses from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Hampton Park Terrace and Wagener Terrace add bungalows, and West Ashley and North Charleston are built largely of post-war ranches, some on slabs in low ground. Summerville, Goose Creek and Ladson provide newer suburban stock.

Across all three regions, crawlspace moisture, termite damage, aging HVAC and original wiring and plumbing are the usual budget drivers. On the coast, flood exposure, rot and salt-air corrosion join the list.

In the Upstate, flips perform well in Greenville's renovated mill villages near the Swamp Rabbit Trail and in the North Main and Augusta Road areas, where buyers pay for careful work on older houses. BRRRR and rental investors focus on ranches in Berea, Parker, Taylors and Wade Hampton and on less-discovered mill villages. Employers such as BMW, Michelin and Prisma Health support steady rental demand.

In the Midlands, Columbia's rental base rests on the University of South Carolina, Fort Jackson, state government and hospitals. Flips work in Shandon, Rosewood, Melrose Heights and Earlewood, while rental and BRRRR investors favor North Columbia, Eau Claire, Dentsville, St. Andrews, West Columbia and Cayce. Student-area duplexes and small buildings near USC and Five Points are a distinct niche.

In the Lowcountry, purchase prices on the Charleston peninsula suit experienced investors with larger budgets and patience for historic review. Upper peninsula, West Ashley and North Charleston flips draw buyers employed at MUSC, Boeing, Joint Base Charleston and the port, and suburban Summerville, Goose Creek and Ladson carry most of the rental activity. Flood insurance can change DSCR math considerably, so it belongs in every coastal analysis.

REO inventory appears statewide, and FHA 203(k) loans help buyers purchase older houses that wouldn't pass a standard FHA appraisal in any of these markets.

sections.h2: Permits, licensing and review in South Carolina
sections.body:
South Carolina adopts building codes statewide through the South Carolina Building Codes Council, and local building departments enforce them. Jurisdiction matters: the City of Columbia, the City of Charleston and the City of Greenville each issue permits within city limits, while counties such as Richland, Charleston and Greenville handle unincorporated areas, and towns like West Columbia, North Charleston, Mount Pleasant, Mauldin and Greer run their own offices. In the Greenville area especially, many addresses sit outside city limits, so confirming the right office is an early step.

Residential contractors must be licensed or registered through the South Carolina Residential Builders Commission, part of the state's Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, and specialty trades carry their own credentials. Permits are generally required for structural work, roofing replacement, electrical, plumbing and mechanical changes, water heaters, additions and decks.

Design review is common in older neighborhoods. Charleston's Board of Architectural Review oversees exterior changes in the city's historic districts, Columbia's Design/Development Review Commission covers its historic and architectural conservation districts, and Greenville's Design Review Board handles its preservation overlays. Coastal properties in FEMA flood hazard areas also face floodplain rules. Lenders typically require a CL-100 wood infestation report before closing. Genstone's field managers coordinate all of it.

sections.h2: Weather and seasonality for South Carolina rehabs
sections.body:
South Carolina's heat and humidity set the tone for nearly every renovation. Columbia's summers rank among the hottest in the Southeast, and long, humid stretches across the state load air conditioners, keep crawlspaces damp and spread mold quickly through vacant houses. Subterranean termites keep feeding through most of the calendar. Those conditions make HVAC sizing, duct sealing, crawlspace moisture control and termite protection core scope items rather than upgrades.

Regional differences matter. The Upstate sees the most ice and snow, and ice storms bring down trees and freeze plumbing in vacant houses. The Midlands gets occasional freezes but is more exposed to heavy rain and flash flooding, as Columbia's October 2015 flood showed. The Lowcountry faces hurricane season from June through November, tidal and rain flooding in low areas and salt air that corrodes equipment and fasteners, with Hugo in 1989 still the benchmark storm.

For scheduling, roofing, siding and exterior paint move most smoothly in spring and fall across the state. Summer favors interior work in conditioned space, and crews often start early to avoid afternoon heat. On the coast, any project with an open roof or removed windows during hurricane season needs a plan to secure the building quickly. In the Upstate, vacant houses need freeze protection through winter.

faqs.q: Which South Carolina markets does Genstone serve?
faqs.a: Our South Carolina work centers on Columbia, Charleston and Greenville, including surrounding towns such as West Columbia, Cayce, Irmo, Lexington, North Charleston, Mount Pleasant, Summerville, Goose Creek, Mauldin, Simpsonville and Greer. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in each market under a designated field manager. If your property is elsewhere in the state, ask, since our contractor network reaches beyond these metros.

faqs.q: What is a CL-100 and why does it matter?
faqs.a: The CL-100 is South Carolina's official wood infestation report, prepared by a licensed pest control company. Most lenders require one before closing on a home purchase, and it notes active infestation and visible damage from termites and other wood-destroying organisms. Because termites are active statewide, our South Carolina scopes include treatment and framing repairs where needed so the property is ready for a clean report before listing or refinancing.

faqs.q: How do flood zones affect South Carolina renovations?
faqs.a: Properties in FEMA flood hazard areas, common around Charleston and along rivers in the Midlands, face floodplain rules, and large renovations or repairs of substantial damage may require raising the house or other compliance work. Flood zone status also drives insurance cost, which affects resale and DSCR calculations. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review flags flood zone status and history so you can price those factors before buying.

faqs.q: Does Genstone have a South Carolina office?
faqs.a: No. Genstone Construction is headquartered in Romeoville, Illinois, and our South Carolina projects are completed by vetted, licensed and insured local contractors. A Genstone field manager runs each job, handling scope, schedule, permits, design review, inspections and documentation. Clients, including out-of-state investors and institutional owners, follow progress through photos and milestones without regular site visits, whether the property is in the Upstate, the Midlands or the Lowcountry.
